reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this manuscript, Chun-Te Ho and colleagues reported that 5hmC levels are higher in young MSCs, promoting MSC
renewal and osteogenesis. They described a mechanism in which the PARP1/TET1 complex hydrolyzes the nucleotide of
Dnmt1 exons to prevent Dnmt1 alternative splicing, producing a DNMT1 variant that suppresses full-length DNMT1. Also,
the stability and nuclear localization of PARP1 are regulated by the ATM/TRIM37 complex. This mechanism is innovative,
and the mouse phenotype is interesting. However, the below major points weaken the rigor of this study.
Major points:
1. This work described an interesting mechanism for the role of TRIM37 in regulating MSC property. However, the major
components in this mechanism, including TET1, DNMT1, and PARP1, all have a wide spectrum of downstream targets in
controlling stemness, proliferation, and senescence. It is unclear how much this linear mechanism, as proposed by the
manuscript -- TRIM37 -> TET1/PARP1 stability and cellular localization –> DNMT1 alternative splicing -- contributes to the
phenotype. To clarify this, many well-controlled rescue experiments are needed, which are lacking here.
2. 2HG was used for TET inhibition in Fig. 1g to show that it produces a phenotype similar to TET1 KO in cell cultures.
However, the specificity of 2HG is in question. 2HG is known to be a key metabolite that promotes several pathways, such
as KDM family histone demethylase function, and broadly affects cellular processes.
3. Vitamin C is widely used to promote in vitro MSC osteogenesis. Besides regulating TET function, it help removing histone
H3K9me3 and K27me3 and can improve collagen production. It is unlikely to act solely via enhancing TET protein function.
4. PJ34 inhibited PARP1 activity by targeting its catalytic domain, preventing the synthesis of PAR polymers, which should
lead to the accumulation of DNA damage and subsequent cellular senescence. Do you see the difference in PAR level
between early and late MSCs?
5. In Fig 1a, the authors detected the global 5hmC level with dot-blot and observed a significant decrease in late MSCs.
However, the dot-blot result of 5mC is not provided and quantified.
6. In line 124, according to the early study, the authors mentioned that the TET1 and TET2 double knockout have lower
5hmC levels in mouse BM-MSCs than the TET1/2KO or control group. TET2-KD 5hmC does not change 5hmC leve1 (Fig
1h), while the expression level of TET2 seems to be higher than that of TET1 in the control MSC (Fig 1g). It is known that
TET1 and TET2 have overlapping functions and exhibit distinct expression patterns in different cellular contexts. It is unclear
whether they target different genes and have a distinct role in MSC. How much TET2 contributes to the MSC properties and
aging was not assessed and discussed further. It would be helpful to have parallel TET2-KD experiments.
7. The bioinformatics data needed to be analyzed and described more sufficiently. How many differentially expressed genes
are observed from the RNA-seq? What are the altered pathways? Are those pathways relevant to the phenotypes? And can
the altered genes in these pathways be clustered well within each group? Does the heatmap of Fig 2C display CPM values
or Z-scores? Additionally, are these values representative of all genes? A batch effect is noted from the late/KD cluster
between donors 1 and 2. The hierarchical clustering showed that the TET1-KD and PARP1-KD tend to be closer to the late
MSC.
8. In line 202, the authors may provide a detailed description of the subgroups of MSC and list the number of genes in each
subset. The supplementary tables are difficult to navigate, so an instruction spreadsheet explaining the contents of each
spreadsheet will be helpful.
9. Extended Data Fig. denotes the colocalized ChIP-seq peaks of PARP1 and TET1 in the genome browser. Is that locus a
TSS; if yes, how is TSS defined here? Please provide the peak coordinate in the browser view and figure legends.
10. The decrease of DNMT1 in PARP1 and TET1 KD suggests the alternative splicing of DNMT1; has this been confirmed
from RNA-seq data -- a genome browser view of the DMNT1 sequence would make this conclusion more convincing.
11. In line 238. The spliced DNMT1 lost the DNMT1 activity. It was also observed that the addition of AS-DNMT1 abrupted
the activity of Full-DNMT1. This observation is interesting but needs further investigation/explanation. Does the
overexpressed AS-DNMT1 change overall DNA methylation, and are those genes related to cellular senescence?
12. Is DNMT1 the only target of this mechanism in alternative splicing? Considering TET1 affects the epigenome broadly, it
is puzzling why only DNMT1 is selected for analysis.
Minor points:
1. In line 65, the authors said, “However, this does not explain why the telomers of cancer cells are paradoxically shorter
than those found in normal tissue.” This seems irrelevant to any part of the results.
2. In line 152, the author mentioned, “PARP1 and TET2 contribute to an epigenetic program ... during somatic cell
reprogramming”, but the objective is to investigate the PAPR1 and TET1 interaction in MSC. Please provide the known
PARP1 and TET1 interaction.
3. In Line 61, “analyzed the related heat maps” may be changed to “we further analyzed the RNA-seq of gene expression
profiles …”. Similarly, in the Method, line 533. The original texts sound like the RNA-seq was only used to generate a
heatmap.
4. Figure legend of Fig 3g, please provide the definition of #1 and #2
5. Line 1099. Please add T203E.
6. Please check text consistency, such as 5hmC vs. 5hmc, 5mC vs.5 mC.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
SIGNIFICANCE
This study attempts to create mechanistic connections between ATM, TRIM37, PARP1, TET1 and CTCF in modulating
methylation of the DNMT1 gene to mediate alternative splicing of DNMT1 to modulate the proliferative properties of MSCs.
CRITIQUE
1. One overall concern is that while the multiple mechanistic connections are theoretically feasible and somewhat supported
by the data, experimental evidence for each connection is of poor quality, not well controlled and generally not compelling.
2. The title severely overstates the findings. This paper does not present any direct data that TRIM37 mitigates osteoporosis.
In fact, nothing in this paper has even a remote bearing on osteoporosis. This problem of overstating the strength of the
evidence is symptomatic for other findings in the paper.
3. TRIM37 has a wide range of cellular activities and molecular functions. Effects on DNMT1 function by modifying
alternative splicing of DNMT1 represents a very specific mechanism that is unlikely to be the only or principal target of
TRIM37.
4. The authors state that “5hmC levels positively regulates MSC self-renewal and osteoblast differentiation, which is at odds
with recent studies in Nat Comm that Vitamin C dependent 5hmC levels promote osteogenesis rather than stemness.
5. All blot based methods (dot blots and western blots) are of very poor quality and these blots cannot be properly quantified.
6. The paper contains a number of avoidable spelling errors and generally does not meet high standards of academic writing
expected for Nature brand papers (e.g., “Westering blotting”?)
7. Extended Data:
a) Experimental evidence for senescence presented (see extended data, Figure 1) is rather minimal and insuffient.
b) The quality of immunoprecipitations (see extended data, Figure 2) is not compelling and lack essential controls. The
resulting conclusion that PARP1, TET1 and CTCF directly interact is not evident from the data shown.
c) The ChIP-seq tracks (see extended data, Figure 3) claim to show TET1 and PARP1 binding to the TSS but there are
upstream exons that are not annotated giving the appearance that the location is intragenic. Input background is high and
the level of enrichment appears to be limited.
d) The compilation of data on effects of TRIM37 and PARP1 on MSC activity (see extended data, Figure 7) is of poor quality
and not convincing.
e) Effects of PARP1 knockout on bone healing in a drill hole model are not quantified and qualitative effects are not
apparent.
f) Supplemental Table 7 shows that only three MSC donors were considered and these donors were neither age nor gender
matched.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point-by-Point Response
Reviewer #1
This is an insightful research focusing on the pathogenetic mechanisms of senescence of
MSCs. This study emphasizes the role of DNA hydroxymethylation in stemness, suggesting
therapeutic strategies, especially for osteoporosis. The authors demonstrate the critical
role of TRIM37/PARP1/DNMT1 pathway by introducing splicing. Additionally, the research
reveals that expansion of MSCs in growth medium containing ATM and TET activators
should be considered in future clinical settings. This manuscript is recommended a major
revision before acceptance.
1. This study focusing on the modification of 5hmC. As we all know, TET1 and DNMT1 also
involve in the modification of 5mC. How about the corresponding change of 5mC in MSCs
when disposed with inhibitors or shRNA. Maybe the authors should claim this at the first
part data to illuminate the change and the relationship with 5hmC.
Response: Thank you very much for your insightful comments. There are no corresponding
changes in 5mC levels in MSCs when treated with TET1 inhibitors or shRNA. Extended Data
Fig. 2b, 2c.
2. When referring to proliferation and differentiation potential of early human MSCs,
osteogenesis and adiposis were performed . Maybe chondrogeneis could be added to
further clarify the differentiation potential of early human MSCs.
Response: Thank you very much for your insightful comments. Chondrogenesis is more
complex. For example, leptin receptor (LepR)+ MSCs isolated from murine bone marrow
give rise to osteoblasts and adipocytes but not chondrocytes1. To date, no single MSC
population has been shown to differentiate into osteoblasts, adipocytes, and chondrocytes
simultaneously. Since our study focuses on MSC senescence both in vitro and in vivo, we
did not include a chondrogenesis assay.
3. The researchers reveal knockdown of CTCF in early MSCs reduced the protein level of
full-length DNMT1 and the mRNA level of DNMT1 in exon 34, but not in exon 13,
suggesting that CTCF knockdown caused alternative splicing. These data indicate the
involvement of CTCF in PARP1/TET1 complex-mediated loss of intragenic DNA methylation
and prevention of DNMT1 alternative splicing in early MSCs. AS is regarded as one
innovative point of this study. The authors should provide more details and data on splicing
mechanism.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. To further investigate the splicing
mechanism, we performed PARP1 and TET1 knockdown in early MSCs. Our results show
that their knockdown reduces CTCF binding to Exon 30 and Exon 37, supporting the role of
CTCF in the PARP1/TET1 complex-mediated regulation of intragenic DNA methylation and
the prevention of DNMT1 alternative splicing in early MSCs (Extended Data Fig. 7).
4. The researchers try to demonstrate the involvement of TRIM37 and PARP1 in MSC aging
in vivo by using young, aged, and TRIM37 KO mice. One point is whether using ATM
activator or vitamin C to old mice or TRIM37 KO mice could rescue the aging process of
mice in vivo? Maybe more experiments in vivo should be performed.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. We have now treated aged mice (75
weeks old) with an ATM activator (resveratrol) and/or a TET activator (vitamin C). Our
findings indicate that the combination treatment enhanced bone parameters, including
BMD, BV/TV, Tb.No., and Tb.Th., while reducing BS/BV and Tb.Sp. Additionally, it improved
bone repair capacity after injury compared to the control and certain single-treatment
groups (Fig. 8).
5. The details of the figure designing could be further improved, such as the color of
statistic panels and the structure of the figures.
Response: Thank you very much for your insightful comments. We have now improved the
color of statistic panels and the structure of the figures, such as Fig. 1a-1d, 1f-1h, Fig. 2d,
2f-2i, Fig. 3i-3n, Fig. 4g-4h, Fig. 5d-5h, and Fig. 7b-7e.
Overall, this is an excellent research which will have a great potential in addressing the
aging problem in future.
Response: Thank you very much for your encouragement.
Reviewer #2
In this paper, the authors showed that the phosphorylation of TRIM37 by ATM promotes
nuclear translocation of PARP1 and protein stabilization. In addition, PARP1 recruits TET1,
which hydrolyzes methylated nucleotides on DNMT1 exons and inhibits alternative splicing
of DNMT1. Bone density was reduced and bone regeneration was impaired in mice lacking
TRIM37 or PARP1. The author demonstrated that TRIM37 and PARP1 are involved in MSC
senescence and bone remodeling, and proposed a meaningful strategy for the treatment of
osteoporosis. Overall, the paper is well organized, but the most important part has already
been reported that PARP1 and TET are involved in the maintenance of stemness. In
addition, there are some questions which need to be addressed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful comment. We acknowledge that the
involvement of PARP1 and TET2 proteins in the maintenance of pluripotency and
reprogramming has been well-documented, particularly in the context of induced
pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) generation. Specifically, the study by Doege et al. (Nature,
2012)2 demonstrated that PARP1 and TET2 are recruited to pluripotency loci such as
Nanog and Esrrb during early reprogramming stages. PARP1 was shown to regulate 5mC
modification, while TET2 catalyzed the conversion of 5mC to 5hmC, facilitating chromatin
remodeling and transcriptional activation of pluripotency genes.
However, our study expands on these earlier findings by uncovering a novel regulatory
mechanism specific to adult stem cells—particularly MSCs. We provide evidence that
TRIM37, through its phosphorylation by ATM, promotes the nuclear translocation and
stabilization of PARP1 in adult MSCs. This process is crucial for the recruitment of TET1 to
specific exons of DNMT1, which regulates alternative splicing and influences MSC identity
and function. This mechanism, not previously identified in the context of MSCs, links DNA
damage response signaling with epigenetic regulation, and highlights a critical pathway in
MSC aging and bone regeneration.
Thus, while previous studies primarily focused on pluripotency induction in the
reprogramming of somatic cells, our work provides a new dimension by revealing how
PARP1 and TET1 cooperate to maintain stemness and regulate MSC function in the context
of aging and bone remodeling. We hope this clarification underscores the novelty of our
findings and their potential relevance to regenerative medicine.
Major point
・ The author should briefly describe the results obtained in this experiment in the
Introduction section.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. “In the current study, we first found
that increased 5hmC levels are required to maintain the early passage characteristics of
human bone marrow (BM)-derived MSCs. We further revealed that CTCF-mediated
prevention of DNMT1 alternative splicing plays a key role in sustaining the proliferative
capacity and differentiation potential of early passage BM-MSCs, which depends on the
coordinated actions of TET1 and DNA damage response (DDR) components such as ATM,
PARP1, and TRIM37. Mechanistically, PARP1 recruits TET1 to demethylate DNMT1 exons,
facilitating CTCF-mediated splicing regulation, while ATM-mediated phosphorylation of
TRIM37 promotes PARP1 stabilization. Knockdown of CTCF or TRIM37 induces replicative
senescence. Importantly, combined treatment with an ATM activator (resveratrol) and a
TET activator (vitamin C) rejuvenates late-passage MSCs, restores osteogenic capacity,
and enhances bone regeneration in aged mice. These findings identify a
TRIM37/PARP1/DNMT1 regulatory axis critical for MSC stemness and bone homeostasis,
suggesting a therapeutic strategy for osteoporosis.” has now added into the introduction
section. Page 6 Line 4-6

・ In Figure 2, the authors claim “PARP1 interacts with TET1 to increase 5hmC levels and

Response: Thank you very much for the comments. We have carefully checked and revised

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Chun-Te Ho and colleagues reported that 5hmC levels are higher in
young MSCs, promoting MSC renewal and osteogenesis. They described a mechanism in
which the PARP1/TET1 complex hydrolyzes the nucleotide of Dnmt1 exons to prevent
Dnmt1 alternative splicing, producing a DNMT1 variant that suppresses full-length DNMT1.
Also, the stability and nuclear localization of PARP1 are regulated by the ATM/TRIM37
complex. This mechanism is innovative, and the mouse phenotype is interesting. However,
the below major points weaken the rigor of this study.
Major points:
1. This work described an interesting mechanism for the role of TRIM37 in regulating MSC
property. However, the major components in this mechanism, including TET1, DNMT1, and
PARP1, all have a wide spectrum of downstream targets in controlling stemness,
proliferation, and senescence. It is unclear how much this linear mechanism, as proposed
by the manuscript -- TRIM37 -> TET1/PARP1 stability and cellular localization –> DNMT1
alternative splicing -- contributes to the phenotype. To clarify this, many well-controlled
rescue experiments are needed, which are lacking here.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments regarding the role of TRIM37 in
regulating MSC properties and the need for well-controlled rescue experiments to support
our proposed mechanism. To address these concerns, we have performed additional
experiments in the new version to clarify the contributions of TRIM37-mediated
stabilization of TET1/PARP1 and DNMT1 alternative splicing to the observed phenotype.
1. Role of TRIM37 Nuclear Relocalization and Phosphorylation (T203) in MSC Function
We investigated the role of T203 phosphorylation in TRIM37 nuclear relocalization and its
functional consequences. Our data show that T203 phosphorylation enhances TRIM37
nuclear localization (Fig. 5h) and short-term proliferation (T203E > WT > T203A)
(Extended Data Fig. 10b). However, nuclear localization does not appear to be the primary
determinant of TRIM37’s function in PARP1 stabilization (Extended Data Fig. 10a) or MSC
differentiation (Extended Data Fig. 10c). Both WT and T203E TRIM37 rescued PARP1
expression and differentiation in TRIM37-KD MSCs, indicating that while phosphorylation
facilitates TRIM37 nuclear relocalization, its role in stabilizing PARP1 and supporting
differentiation is largely independent of nuclear localization efficiency. These findings
suggest that distinct mechanisms regulate TRIM37’s effects on proliferation and
differentiation.
2. PARP1/TET1 and CTCF Regulation of DNMT1 Alternative Splicing
To further investigate the splicing mechanism, we performed PARP1 and TET1 knockdown
in early MSCs and analyzed CTCF binding at DNMT1 Exon 30 and Exon 37. Our results
show that knockdown of PARP1 and TET1 reduces CTCF binding at these sites, supporting
the role of the PARP1/TET1 complex in regulating intragenic DNA methylation and
preventing DNMT1 alternative splicing in early MSCs (Extended Data Fig. 7). These
findings provide mechanistic evidence that TRIM37-mediated stabilization of PARP1 and
TET1 contributes to DNMT1 splicing regulation and, consequently, MSC function. In these
experiments, we used scrambled shRNA as a control for shRNA against PARP1 and TET1,
and H19 served as a control for Exon 30 and Exon 37.
3. Functional Relationship Between PARP1 and TET1 in MSCs
To clarify the interdependence of PARP1 and TET1 in regulating MSC properties, we
overexpressed PARP1 in late MSCs and performed TET1 knockdown. Our results
demonstrate that TET1 knockdown suppresses the effects of PARP1 overexpression on
senescence marker expression (Extended Data Fig. 5a), 5hmC levels (Extended Data Fig.
5b), proliferation capacity (Extended Data Fig. 5c), and differentiation potential
(Extended Data Fig. 5d). These findings confirm the functional relationship between PARP1
and TET1 in regulating early MSC properties, further supporting the mechanistic pathway we
propose. In these experiments, we used scrambled shRNA as a control for shRNA against
TET1.
Together, these results reinforce that TRIM37 regulates MSC properties via stabilization of
PARP1/TET1 and modulation of DNMT1 alternative splicing. While additional regulatory
mechanisms may contribute to MSC function, our data demonstrate that this pathway
plays a significant role in the observed phenotype.
We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion for further validation, and we believe these
additional data strengthen our conclusions.
2. 2HG was used for TET inhibition in Fig. 1g to show that it produces a phenotype similar
to TET1 KO in cell cultures. However, the specificity of 2HG is in question. 2HG is known to
be a key metabolite that promotes several pathways, such as KDM family histone
demethylase function, and broadly affects cellular processes.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. While 2HG was used as a TET inhibitor
in Fig. 1g to demonstrate a phenotype similar to TET1 KO, we acknowledge that its
specificity is in question, as 2HG also inhibits KDM family histone demethylases in addition
to TET enzymes, broadly affecting cellular processes. Both TET and KDM enzymes are
Fe(II)/α-KG-dependent dioxygenases involved in epigenetic regulation—TET enzymes
regulate DNA demethylation, while KDM demethylases modify histone methylation.
Notably, TET1 has been shown to interact with KDM2A and KDM6A, suggesting coordinated
regulation of DNA and histone methylation. Given that 2HG inhibits both TET and KDM
enzymes, the observed phenotype could result from broader epigenetic effects rather than
TET inhibition alone. To address this concern, we performed TET1 knockdown experiments,
which confirmed that TET1, rather than TET2, is the primary enzyme responsible for
increasing 5hmC levels.
3. Vitamin C is widely used to promote in vitro MSC osteogenesis. Besides regulating TET
function, it helps removing histone H3K9me3 and K27me3 and can improve collagen
production. It is unlikely to act solely via enhancing TET protein function.
Response: Thank you very much for your insightful comments. Our current study
highlights the critical role of TET1 in intragenic DNA demethylation, which is essential for
maintaining MSC stemness during early MSC culture. Vitamin C enhances TET-mediated
5hmC DNA hydroxymethylation at the promoters, enhancers, and super-enhancers of
bone-specific genes, and it also regulates histone demethylation of H3K9me3 and
H3K27me35. Notably, the deletion of the 5hmC writers, TET1 and TET2, in vitamin C-
sufficient murine bone leads to severe skeletal defects that closely resemble those seen in
vitamin C-deficient Gulo knockout mice, despite the preservation of normal histone
demethylation5. These findings challenge the sufficiency of histone demethylation in
maintaining bone growth and skeletal integrity, emphasizing that vitamin C’s role in
osteogenesis extends beyond its impact on TET protein function alone.
4. PJ34 inhibited PARP1 activity by targeting its catalytic domain, preventing the synthesis
of PAR polymers, which should lead to the accumulation of DNA damage and subsequent
cellular senescence. Do you see the difference in PAR level between early and late MSCs?
Response: Thank you for your comment. We observed that PAR levels in murine MSCs
from 24-week-old mice were significantly lower than those from 4- or 8-week-old mice
(Extended Data Fig. 11a). Although PJ34 treatment effectively reduced TET1 PARylation by
inhibiting PARP1’s catalytic activity and blocking PAR polymer synthesis, it did not disrupt
the interaction between TET1, PARP1, and CTCF (Extended Data Fig. 3). These findings
suggest that TET1 associates with PARP1 and CTCF independently of PARP1’s enzymatic
function.
While PJ34 treatment may potentially lead to increased DNA damage and subsequent
cellular senescence due to impaired PARP1 function, the treatment duration in our
experiments was short-term. As a result, we did not observe overt signs of DNA damage or
senescence within this timeframe.
5. In Fig 1a, the authors detected the global 5hmC level with dot-blot and observed a
significant decrease in late MSCs. However, the dot-blot result of 5mC is not provided and
quantified.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. We have now provided and quantified
the dot-blot results for 5mC in early and late MSCs (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Our analyses
revealed an increase in 5hmC levels in early MSCs, as shown by both immunofluorescence
(Fig. 1a) and dot-blot assays (Extended Data Fig. 2a). In contrast, 5mC levels were
elevated in late MSCs (Extended Data Fig. 2a, Fig. 1a), aligning with findings from previous
studies6,7.
6. In line 124, according to the early study, the authors mentioned that the TET1 and TET2
double knockout have lower 5hmC levels in mouse BM-MSCs than the TET1/2KO or control
group. TET2-KD 5hmC does not change 5hmC level (Fig 1h), while the expression level of
TET2 seems to be higher than that of TET1 in the control MSC (Fig 1g). It is known that
TET1 and TET2 have overlapping functions and exhibit distinct expression patterns in
different cellular contexts. It is unclear whether they target different genes and have a
distinct role in MSC. How much TET2 contributes to the MSC properties and aging was not
assessed and discussed further. It would be helpful to have parallel TET2-KD experiments.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. We appreciate the reviewer's
suggestion regarding the importance of performing TET2 knockdown experiments in
parallel with TET1 knockdown to fully dissect their roles in early MSC properties. Our
current data already provide strong evidence that TET1, but not TET2, knockdown
significantly reduces 5hmC levels, as demonstrated by both immunofluorescence and dot
blot analysis. While dot blot suggests that both TET1 and TET2 knockdowns reduce 5hmC,
the immunofluorescence results indicate a more prominent effect for TET1. These results
suggest that TET1 plays a dominant role in regulating 5hmC levels in MSCs.
The discrepancy between immunofluorescence and dot blot results in TET2 knockdown
likely arises due to differences in detection sensitivity and the nature of the assays. Dot
blot provides a global, quantitative measurement of total 5hmC levels and is more
sensitive to small reductions, whereas immunofluorescence captures regional 5hmC
distribution and may not detect subtle, widespread changes. This suggests that TET2
influences 5hmC at a genome-wide level but does not cause strong focal reductions in
nuclear 5hmC staining. Given that TET1 knockdown significantly affects both dot blot and
immunofluorescence, our results support the dominant role of TET1 in regulating 5hmC in
MSCs.
Performing additional TET2 knockdown experiments in early MSCs would be a substantial
undertaking, requiring extensive time and resources. Given that our key findings
emphasize TET1’s role, we believe our current data sufficiently support our conclusions.
However, if the reviewer considers Tet2’s contribution critical to our study’s main
conclusions, we could consider conducting a limited set of TET2 knockdown experiments in
MSCs in future follow-up studies.
7. The bioinformatics data needed to be analyzed and described more sufficiently. How
many differentially expressed genes are observed from the RNA-seq? What are the altered
pathways? Are those pathways relevant to the phenotypes? And can the altered genes in
these pathways be clustered well within each group? Does the heatmap of Fig 2C display
CPM values or Z-scores? Additionally, are these values representative of all genes? A batch
effect is noted from the late/KD cluster between donors 1 and 2. The hierarchical
clustering showed that the TET1-KD and PARP1-KD tend to be closer to the late MSC.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. The analysis of the RNA-seq data is
described in details in the Method section in the revised manuscript. There are 1026
differentially expressed genes (DGEs) by comparing early MSCs to late MSCs from the
three donors. Pathway analysis of these DGEs revealed several altered pathways that are
responsible for the early MSC phenotypes. The top 20 activated biological functions,
including differentiation of osteoblast and adipogenesis of cells, and top 20 suppressed
biological functions are presented in Extended Data Fig. 4 in the revision. Moreover, the
enrichment of the DGEs in the altered pathways within each group is evident by P-value
(Dataset S1). The heatmap of Fig. 2c displays Z-scores and the information is stated in the
Figure legend. We recognize the individual difference among the three donors, especially
donor 3 has a quite distinct expression profile from donors 1 and 2. Interestingly, donor 3
is older than donor 1 and donor 2 (Table S7). Although batch effect did exit when RNA-seq
assays were performed in different flow cells, the TET1-KD and PARP1-KD tending to be
closer to the late MSCs is more relevant to biological effect than batch effect, as the early
MSC, late MSC, TET1-KD, and PARP1-KD of donor 1 were subjected to NGS in the same
flow cell. In Figure 2c, the hierarchical clustering showed that the TET1-KD and PARP1-KD
tend to be closer to the late MSCs of donor 1 or 2, strongly suggesting that knocking down
these genes may drive MSCs toward a late-stage phenotype.
8. In line 202, the authors may provide a detailed description of the subgroups of MSC and
list the number of genes in each subset. The supplementary tables are difficult to navigate,
so an instruction spreadsheet explaining the contents of each spreadsheet will be helpful.
Response: Thank you very much for the helpful comments. We have provided a schematic
diagram for each subset in Supplementary Table 2 to aid interpretation, following the
format used in a previous study8. Supplementary Table 2 includes the counts of five types
of alternative splicing events identified by rMATS: SE (skipped exon), A5SS (alternative 5′
splice site), A3SS (alternative 3′ splice site), MXE (mutually exclusive exons), and RI
(retained intron). Please note that the analysis was performed using a cutoff of FDR < 0.05
and |ΔPSI| > 0.1. To improve usability, we will also provide an instruction sheet for
Supplementary Table 2, as well as Datasets S2, S3, and S4, summarizing the contents and
structure of each spreadsheet.
9. Extended Data Fig. denotes the colocalized ChIP-seq peaks of PARP1 and TET1 in the
genome browser. Is that locus a TSS; if yes, how is TSS defined here? Please provide the
peak coordinate in the browser view and figure legends.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. The transcription start site (TSS for
DNMT1 was defined based on the first nucleotide of the mRNA that corresponds to the
5’UTR according to the RefSeq database (NM_001130823.3; chr19:10305629). In
Extended Data Fig. 6, the DNA region of promoter, exon 1, and part of intron 1 of the
DNMT1 gene is enlarged to show physical coordinate of TSS flanking region and ChIP-seq
peaks. We have also revised the figure legends: Extended Data Fig. 6. PARP1 and TET1
ChIP-seq analysis revealed that the flanking region of transcription start site (TSS, Chr19:
10305629) of DNMT1 was enriched with PARP1 and TET1 in early MSCs.
10. The decrease of DNMT1 in PARP1 and TET1 KD suggests the alternative splicing of
DNMT1; has this been confirmed from RNA-seq data -- a genome browser view of the
DMNT1 sequence would make this conclusion more convincing.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. We performed genome browser
analysis of the DNMT1 locus using RNA-seq data in Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV), but
did not observe any promising alternatively spliced transcripts. One possible explanation is
that the alternatively spliced DNMT1 transcripts were not stable and therefore not captured
by RNA-seq. Consistently, Western blotting of cell lysates from early and late MSCs, with or
without pretreatment with MG132, also failed to detect this isoform (Extended Data Fig.
9), further suggesting that the mRNA or protein isoform is unstable.
11. In line 238. The spliced DNMT1 lost the DNMT1 activity. It was also observed that the
addition of AS-DNMT1 abrupted the activity of Full-DNMT1. This observation is interesting
but needs further investigation/explanation. Does the overexpressed AS-DNMT1 change
overall DNA methylation, and are those genes related to cellular senescence?
Response: Thank you very much for the thoughtful comments. Compared to the control
vector (CV), overexpression of AS-DNMT1 led to a reduction in global 5mC levels in 293T
cells (Fig. 3j), suggesting a dominant-negative effect on DNA methylation. Consistently, in
MSCs, AS-DNMT1 overexpression resulted in upregulation of the senescence-associated
genes p21 and p16, along with impaired proliferation and differentiation potential
compared to CV (Fig. 3k–3m). These genes, p21 and p16, are canonical markers of cellular
senescence. Their upregulation in AS-DNMT1–overexpressing MSCs supports the idea that
AS-DNMT1 contributes to senescence-associated phenotypes through epigenetic
deregulation. These findings indicate that AS-DNMT1 may functionally interfere with full-
length DNMT1, potentially linking alternative splicing to stem cell aging. Further
mechanistic studies are warranted to elucidate the precise pathways involved.
12. Is DNMT1 the only target of this mechanism in alternative splicing? Considering TET1
affects the epigenome broadly, it is puzzling why only DNMT1 is selected for analysis.
Response: Thank you very much for the insightful comments. We agree that TET1 broadly
influences the epigenome and may impact the splicing of multiple genes. To identify
potential targets, we examined CTCF binding motifs within the regions showing triple
overlapping enrichment from MeDIP-seq, PARP1 ChIP-seq, and TET1 ChIP-seq, which
yielded 20 candidate genes (Table S3). Among these, DNMT1 and LPA (Lipoprotein A)
exhibited the highest number of predicted CTCF motifs. We chose to focus on DNMT1
because of its well-established role in maintaining mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)
stemness, a key factor in preserving stem cell identity3. While other genes may also be
involved, DNMT1 was prioritized due to its strong functional relevance to our study.
Minor points:
1. In line 65, the authors said, “However, this does not explain why the telomers of cancer
cells are paradoxically shorter than those found in normal tissue.” This seems irrelevant to
any part of the results.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. We have now deleted this description
in the revised version.
2. In line 152, the author mentioned, “PARP1 and TET2 contribute to an epigenetic
program ... during somatic cell reprogramming”, but the objective is to investigate the
PAPR1 and TET1 interaction in MSC. Please provide the known PARP1 and TET1 interaction.
Response: Thank you very much for your valuable comment. We have now included
previous studies that describe the interaction between PARP1 and TET1. “For instance, it
has been reported that PARP1 facilitates the establishment of H3K4me3 marks at the TET1
promoter and directly interacts with TET1, contributing to the progression of T-cell acute
lymphoblastic leukemia9” Please refer to Page 9 Line 8 – Page 9 Line11.
3. In Line 61, “analyzed the related heat maps” may be changed to “we further analyzed
the RNA-seq of gene expression profiles …”. Similarly, in the Method, line 533. The original
texts sound like the RNA-seq was only used to generate a heatmap.
Response: Thank you very much for the insightful comment. We have revised the
manuscript accordingly. Specifically, the sentence in Line 61 has been modified to “we
further analyzed the RNA-seq of gene expression profiles…” to better reflect the scope of
the analysis. In the Methods section, the original title “RNA-seq analysis for heatmap” has
been revised to “RNA-seq and transcriptomic data analysis” to clarify that the RNA-seq
data were used for comprehensive transcriptomic analysis, not solely for generating
heatmaps. Please refer to Page 33 Line 6.
4. Figure legend of Fig 3g, please provide the definition of #1 and #2
Response: Thank you very much for the helpful comment. We have revised the figure
legend in the manuscript to clarify that “#1” and “#2” refer to two different shRNA
constructs targeting CTCF.
5. Line 1099. Please add T203E.
Response: Thank you very much for the comments. We have revised them in the Figure 5h
legend in the revised manuscript.
6. Please check text consistency, such as 5hmC vs. 5hmc, 5mC vs.5 mC.
Response: Thank you very much for your comment. We have carefully revised the
manuscript to ensure consistency in the formatting of terms such as 5mC and 5hmC.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
SIGNIFICANCE
This study attempts to create mechanistic connections between ATM, TRIM37, PARP1,
TET1 and CTCF in modulating methylation of the DNMT1 gene to mediate alternative
splicing of DNMT1 to modulate the proliferative properties of MSCs.
CRITIQUE
1. One overall concern is that while the multiple mechanistic connections are theoretically
feasible and somewhat supported by the data, experimental evidence for each connection
is of poor quality, not well controlled and generally not compelling.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the quality, control, and
strength of the experimental evidence supporting our proposed mechanistic connections.
In response to this overarching critique—as well as to specific comments from all four
reviewers—we have extensively revised the manuscript to significantly enhance both the
rigor and clarity of our findings.
Specifically, we have conducted additional well-controlled experiments to directly address
each mechanistic link. For example:
The levels of 5hmC and 5mC, originally detected by immunofluorescence, are now further
validated using dot-blot analysis with quantification (Extended Data Fig. 2).
We demonstrate that re-expression of shRNA-resistant TRIM37 wild-type (WT) and T203E
mutant restore PARP1 expression, as well as MSC proliferation and differentiation capacity,
while expression of the T203A mutant does not (Extended Data Fig. 10).
We treated aged mice (75 weeks old) with an ATM activator (resveratrol) and/or a TET
activator (vitamin C). This combinatorial treatment significantly improved bone
parameters—such as BMD, BV/TV, Tb.N, and Tb.Th—and reduced BS/BV and Tb.Sp.
Moreover, it enhanced bone repair following injury compared to both control and single-
treatment groups (Fig. 8).
These additional data now provide strong, experimentally substantiated support for the
mechanistic model proposed. We have also strengthened the statistical analyses and
quantification throughout.
We believe these comprehensive revisions have substantially improved the manuscript.
The experiments are now rigorously controlled, the results are robust, and the mechanistic
conclusions are compelling.
2. The title severely overstates the findings. This paper does not present any direct data
that TRIM37 mitigates osteoporosis. In fact, nothing in this paper has even a remote
bearing on osteoporosis. This problem of overstating the strength of the evidence is
symptomatic for other findings in the paper.
Response: We respectfully disagree with the reviewer’s statement that our findings lack
relevance to osteoporosis. Our in vivo data clearly support the conclusion that TRIM37 is
critical not only for maintaining skeletal homeostasis and preventing age-related bone loss,
but also for preserving bone repair capacity—both of which are hallmark features of
osteoporosis.
First, TRIM37-deficient mice exhibit a pronounced osteoporotic phenotype, characterized
by significant reductions in bone mineral density (BMD), bone volume fraction (BV/TV),
and trabecular number (Tb.N), along with increased trabecular separation (Tb.Sp) (Fig.
7b). Furthermore, these mice show impaired bone repair capacity following cortical bone
injury (Fig. 7e).
Second, and importantly, TRIM37 deficiency compromises the bone’s intrinsic ability to
heal. In a cortical defect model, TRIM37-deficient mice demonstrated delayed bone
healing. However, treatment of aged mice (75 weeks old) with an ATM activator
(resveratrol) and/or a TET activator (vitamin C) not only improved structural bone
parameters (BMD, BV/TV, Tb.N, Tb.Th, BS/BV, Tb.Sp) (Fig. 8a), but also significantly
enhanced bone regeneration at the defect site compared to vehicle or single-agent
treatments (Fig. 8b). Notably, the combination treatment led to the greatest improvement
in bone repair capacity following cortical injury (Fig. 8c).
Together, these findings provide compelling biological and functional evidence that TRIM37
deficiency contributes to an osteoporosis-like condition, and that modulation of the
downstream ATM/TET pathway can partially rescue both bone loss and regenerative
deficits. We believe the current title accurately reflects the significance of our study,
though we remain open to revising it should the editors prefer a more conservative
phrasing.
3. TRIM37 has a wide range of cellular activities and molecular functions. Effects on
DNMT1 function by modifying alternative splicing of DNMT1 represents a very specific
mechanism that is unlikely to be the only or principal target of TRIM37.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the diverse functions of
TRIM37 and the specificity of its effects on DNMT1. However, we respectfully submit that
our data clearly demonstrate a mechanistically specific and functionally significant role for
TRIM37 in regulating PARP1 stability through mono-ubiquitination at K337, and that this
process is critically dependent on phosphorylation of TRIM37 at T203.
To identify upstream regulators of PARP1, we performed immunoprecipitation-coupled
mass spectrometry (IP-MS/MS), which revealed phospho-TRIM37 (T203) as one of the
most enriched phosphoproteins associated with PARP1 in early MSCs (Fig. 4a). This
interaction was confirmed biochemically in 293T cells co-transfected with Flag-TRIM37 and
HA-PARP1 (Fig. 4b). As TRIM37 is known to function as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, we
examined whether it ubiquitinates PARP1. Our data demonstrate that TRIM37 mediates
mono-ubiquitination of PARP1 specifically at Lys337 (Fig. 4c), and that this modification
stabilizes PARP1.
Importantly, this mono-ubiquitination and stabilization require phosphorylation of TRIM37
at T203. In 293T cells, the non-phosphorylatable T203A mutant showed markedly reduced
ability to bind, ubiquitinate, and stabilize PARP1, while the phosphomimetic T203E mutant
significantly enhanced these processes (Fig. 4d–e). Moreover, in functional rescue
experiments using TRIM37-knockdown MSCs, only re-expression of wild-type or T203E
TRIM37—not T203A—restored PARP1 protein levels, enhanced proliferation, reduced
senescence, and rescued osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation (Extended Data Fig.
10). These findings firmly establish that T203 phosphorylation is not a secondary or non-
specific event, but is essential for TRIM37’s role in regulating PARP1 function and
downstream MSC biology.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that ATM kinase acts upstream by promoting TRIM37
phosphorylation at T203, enhancing its nuclear localization and interaction with PARP1.
Early-passage MSCs display higher levels of activated ATM, TRIM37, and nuclear PARP1
compared to late-passage MSCs (Fig. 5a–e). Proximity ligation assays confirm enhanced
nuclear association of TRIM37 with both phospho-ATM and PARP1 (Fig. 5f–
g). Pharmacological activation of ATM by resveratrol further increased this nuclear complex
formation. Conversely, overexpression of the T203A TRIM37 mutant impaired nuclear
translocation of TRIM37, while the T203E mutant promoted it (Fig. 5h).
Taken together, these data provide compelling mechanistic evidence that phosphorylation
of TRIM37 at T203 is a critical regulatory event that enables its E3 ligase activity toward
PARP1 at K337, thereby stabilizing PARP1 and supporting MSC proliferation and
differentiation. This mechanism operates independently of TRIM37’s other functions and
highlights a highly specific, ATM-regulated pathway central to MSC function and
senescence.
4. The authors state that “5hmC levels positively regulates MSC self-renewal and
osteoblast differentiation, which is at odds with recent studies in Nat Comm that Vitamin C
dependent 5hmC levels promote osteogenesis rather than stemness.
Response: Our results showed that old female mice daily administrated with Vit C and
resveratrol only promoted osteogenesis but not adipogenesis in vivo, however MSCs
treated with Vit C and resveratrol promoted both osteogenesis and adipogenesis in vitro
(direct effect).
1. Vitamin C Enhances the Generation of Mouse and Human Induced Pluripotent Stem
Cells. Cell Stem Cell 1: 71-79, 2010.
2. Ascorbic acid phosphate stimulates type IV collagen synthesis and accelerates adipose
conversion of 3T3-L1 cells. Experimental Cell Research. Volume 187, Issue 2, April
1990, Pages 309-314.
3. Effect of ascorbic acid on bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cell proliferation
and differentiation. Journal of Bioscience and Bioengineering.
105: 586-594, 2008. Figure 7 & 8
5. All blot based methods (dot blots and western blots) are of very poor quality and these
blots cannot be properly quantified.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s feedback regarding the quality and
quantification of our blot-based methods. We have carefully reviewed our data and have
now quantified all dot blot results using densitometric analysis with appropriate
normalization controls (Extended Data Fig. 2). These quantified data are now included in
the revised manuscript to improve clarity and rigor. We hope this addresses the reviewer’s
concern and appreciate the opportunity to further strengthen our study.
6. The paper contains a number of avoidable spelling errors and generally does not meet
high standards of academic writing expected for Nature brand papers (e.g., “Westering
blotting”?)
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback regarding the language and presentation
of our manuscript. We have carefully proofread the revised version to correct any spelling
errors, including the mentioned typo, and have improved the overall clarity and readability
to meet the high standards expected for Nature-brand papers. We sincerely thank the
reviewer for highlighting this, as it has helped us further refine our manuscript.
7. Extended Data:
a) Experimental evidence for senescence presented (see extended data, Figure 1) is rather
minimal and insufficient.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. To more comprehensively
demonstrate senescence in late-passage MSCs, we have expanded our experimental
validation and clarified the evidence provided in Extended Data Fig. 1, which now includes
multiple, widely accepted hallmarks of cellular senescence:
Morphological changes (Fig. 1a): Late-passage MSCs exhibit enlarged and flattened
morphology, a classical feature of senescent cells.
Senescence markers (Fig. 1b): Western blot analysis shows a consistent decrease in
DNMT1 and an increase in p16Ink4a and p21Waf1/Cip1, both well-established markers of
senescence.
Functional decline (Fig. 1c–d): Late-passage MSCs display reduced proliferation and
impaired differentiation potential into osteoblasts and adipocytes, both indicative of cellular
aging.
Transcriptomic evidence (Fig. 1e): RNA-seq analysis followed by GSEA reveals significant
enrichment of the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) pathway in late-
passage MSCs.
Secretory profile (Fig. 1f): Conditioned medium from late MSCs shows elevated secretion
of key SASP components, including IL-1α and CXCL-8, as measured by ELISA.
SA-β-galactosidase activity (Fig. 1g): Increased SA-β-gal⁺ cell percentage in late MSCs
further confirms senescence at the cellular level.
Together, these multiple independent lines of evidence (morphological, molecular,
functional, transcriptomic, and biochemical) provide a robust and multidimensional
characterization of senescence in late-passage MSCs. We hope this additional clarification
and the strengthened figure address the reviewer’s concern comprehensively.
b) The quality of immunoprecipitations (see extended data, Figure 2) is not compelling and
lack essential controls. The resulting conclusion that PARP1, TET1 and CTCF directly
interact is not evident from the data shown.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful and constructive comment. In
Extended Data Fig. 3, we show that anti-TET1 immunoprecipitates both PARP1 and CTCF,
with consistent results observed under both control and PJ34-treated conditions.
Additionally, Fig. 2a includes a co-immunoprecipitation experiment supporting the
interaction between PARP1 and TET1. IgG immunoprecipitations were included as negative
controls to assess nonspecific binding.
We acknowledge, however, that co-immunoprecipitation does not distinguish between
direct and indirect interactions. To further address this, we are currently performing
proximity ligation assays (PLA) to visualize the spatial proximity of endogenous PARP1,
TET1, and CTCF in situ. In untreated cells, PLA signals for TET1–PARP1 and TET1–CTCF are
primarily nuclear, whereas PJ34 treatment leads to additional cytoplasmic PLA signals. This
cytoplasmic redistribution upon PARP1 inhibition is consistent with observations reported in
previous studies 10. While this redistribution may reflect a disruption of nuclear retention or
chromatin association—potentially due to PARP1’s role in stabilizing chromatin interactions
and anchoring nuclear proteins, such as TET1 and CTCF—we would like to emphasize that
the underlying mechanism of this relocalization is beyond the scope of the present study
and will not be further investigated. Nevertheless, we will include these additional PLA
results in the revised manuscript or supplementary materials (Extended Data Fig. 3b) to
provide stronger support for the spatial proximity and potential interaction among PARP1,
TET1, and CTCF.
c) The ChIP-seq tracks (see extended data, Figure 3) claim to show TET1 and PARP1
binding to the TSS but there are upstream exons that are not annotated giving the
appearance that the location is intragenic. Input background is high and the level of
enrichment appears to be limited.
Response: We thank the reviewer for their insightful comments regarding the ChIP-seq
tracks shown in Extended Data Fig. 6 in the revised version. We would like to clarify and
address the points raised as follows:
First, regarding transcript annotation: we acknowledge that the DNMT1 gene locus
contains alternative upstream exons and TSSs that are not consistently annotated in all
genome builds or databases. In the updated figure, we now include expanded RefSeq
transcript tracks, which show that the observed PARP1 and TET1 binding peaks
(highlighted in orange) are located immediately upstream of exon 1 of a major DNMT1
isoform, and thus are consistent with proximal promoter and TSS binding, not intragenic
binding.
Second, we appreciate the comment regarding the appearance of intragenic binding. The
earlier visual ambiguity was due in part to limited annotation in the displayed tracks. We
have corrected this in the revised figure, which supports that the peaks align with the
canonical promoter region.
Third, concerning input signal and background, we recognize that the input tracks showed
moderate baseline levels. To improve clarity, we have now reprocessed the ChIP-seq data
with normalized tracks and adjusted dynamic ranges. Importantly, ChIP enrichment over
input is clearly seen in both TET1 and PARP1 tracks compared to the corresponding inputs,
especially at the promoter region of DNMT1 (highlighted in orange).
Lastly, while the absolute enrichment may appear modest, we note that TET1 and PARP1
are chromatin regulators with generally broader and lower-amplitude binding profiles,
which is consistent with previous reports 11,12. Nevertheless, we agree with the reviewer
that careful presentation is necessary, and we have now updated the figure and legend to
clearly indicate TSS positions, highlight the peak regions, and explain the biological
relevance of these binding events.
We hope these clarifications and figure revisions adequately address the reviewer’s
concern and improve the transparency and rigor of our ChIP-seq analysis.
d) The compilation of data on effects of TRIM37 and PARP1 on MSC activity (see extended
data, Figure 7) is of poor quality and not convincing.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We acknowledge
that the original data presented in Extended Data Figure 7 may not have been of sufficient
quality to convincingly support the conclusions regarding the roles of TRIM37 and PARP1 in
MSC activity. In response to this concern, we have significantly revised and expanded our
dataset. The updated and more robust data are now presented in Figure 4 and Extended
Data Figures 10 and 11.
In these new figures, we show that lentiviral knockdown of TRIM37 using two independent
shRNAs led to decreased PARP1 and full-length DNMT1 protein levels, increased expression
of senescence markers (Fig. 4f), impaired cell proliferation (Fig. 4g), and reduced
osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation capacity (Fig. 4h) compared to scrambled shRNA
controls.
To further strengthen our mechanistic insight, we performed rescue experiments using
shRNA-resistant constructs encoding wild-type (WT), T203A (non-phosphorylatable), or
T203E (phosphomimetic) TRIM37 in TRIM37-knockdown MSCs. Re-expression of WT or
T203E TRIM37 restored PARP1 expression, reduced senescence marker expression, and
rescued both proliferation and differentiation potentials. In contrast, the T203A mutant
failed to rescue these phenotypes (Extended Data Fig. 10), highlighting the functional
importance of T203 phosphorylation in TRIM37-mediated regulation of MSC biology.
To address the in vivo relevance, we isolated minimally expanded BM-MSCs from young
(<8 weeks) and older (6–10 months) B6 mice. Western blotting revealed age-associated
decreases in TRIM37, PARP1, PAR, and DNMT1, along with increased levels of p16Ink4a and
p21Waf1/Cip1 (Extended Data Fig. 11a, b). Furthermore, BM-MSCs isolated from TRIM37- or
PARP1-deficient mice exhibited reduced TRIM37, PARP1, and DNMT1 protein levels,
elevated senescence markers (Extended Data Fig. 11c–f), and significantly impaired
proliferation (Extended Data Fig. 11g, h) and differentiation potential (Extended Data Fig.
11i, j) compared to WT controls.
Collectively, these improved and extended datasets provide compelling evidence for the
role of TRIM37 and PARP1 in regulating MSC senescence and functional decline both in
vitro and in vivo.
e) Effects of PARP1 knockout on bone healing in a drill hole model are not quantified and
qualitative effects are not apparent.
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the assessment of bone healing
in the drill hole model. To address this concern, we have now included quantitative analysis
of new bone formation using fluorescent densitometry of calcein labeling, as presented in
